extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters and city editors (especially reporters who cover accidents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporters on gathering, verifying, and writing newspaper stories about accidents (automobile crashes, drownings, train wrecks, fires), including when to send photographers, how to handle names and witness statements, attribution and libel-avoidance, and what facts to collect for major wrecks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photograph selection and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictures are merited only for unusual phases or notable circumstances (e.g., a youngster given a car, a senator injured, a machine that turned over four times); otherwise a wreck probably must be fatal to justify a photograph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: City editor must be told quickly so a cameraman can be found; photographers may be busy and wrecked cars may be towed away so the best shot can be lost or reduced to an unattractive garage background. Warn make-up editor and engraver of a rush job.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate collection of names
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of perpetual uncertainty at accident scenes, names must be collected at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get names from police, registration plates, letters in pockets, ambulance drivers, etc., then telephone them to the office for verification. Be prepared for half an hour of telephoning and interviewing to resolve ambiguous identifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrupulous verification of identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever names police offer or indications from registration/letters, these names are to be checked scrupulously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check directory listings, car registration records, hospital lists and interview multiple sources before publishing a specific name; avoid printing until identification is confirmed to prevent causing families needless anguish (example of wrong name 'Henry D. Alden').

rubrics_metrics.name: Label unverified identifications as tentative with reason
rubrics_metrics.description: If names cannot be verified conclusively, give them as 'tentative' and present the reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use phrasing such as: 'Police believe the driver was George H. Jackson, 212 Miami Avenue, because of letters found in a coat in the car.' Explain the basis of the tentative ID and the possibility of error (e.g., car lent to a friend).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on speedometer needle as speed evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not estimate a car's speed by the place at which the speedometer needle jammed because the needle can hop around on impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude such speculative indicators from reconstruction unless corroborated by reliable evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualify witness and victim statements; expect inaccuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediate statements of witnesses or victims cannot be relied upon because excitement may have upset persons so they hardly know what they say; such statements are printable but must be warned as possibly inexact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote the speaker and qualify the statement (e.g., 'Mrs. Henshaw ... told police that her husband had been driving about 85 miles an hour') and present contradictory versions impartially and objectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not allocate blame on-the-spot
rubrics_metrics.description: Never, whatever the circumstances, allocate blame or responsibility in an on-the-spot accident story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid implying culpability from immediate testimony or impressions; wait for official investigations. Use neutral phrasing that does not assign fault until an authorized agency reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only attribute blame with an official report or clear source
rubrics_metrics.description: Blame should not be allocated without an official report from an authorized investigating agency; details of 'what happened' should be attributed to the persons furnishing them except when the action is indisputably clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faulty: 'Engineer Greeley ran by the flagman's signals without slackening the speed of his train.' Acceptable: 'Although a flagman had been dispatched to halt his train, Engineer Greeley was unable to stop in time.' Or attribute: 'State Traffic Patrolman Henry D. Ellis said that apparently Marchand's car sideswiped the Haynes machine...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Present contradictory versions impartially and objectively
rubrics_metrics.description: When witnesses give conflicting accounts, present both sides without favoring one; do not cut down one testimony to exalt another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote each party and avoid editorializing; preserve balance and leave allocation of blame to the law or investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not impute intoxication from circumstantial evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should not impute intoxication to a driver however many whiskey bottles may be found in the car because shock and drunkenness can appear deceptively alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid asserting intoxication unless confirmed by authoritative sources; maintain restraint in speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prompt: keep city editor informed and do not linger
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must inform the city editor promptly of a story's status; do not linger at the scene and miss information or coordination (e.g., photographs, hospital updates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call in frequently rather than remain away for long periods; be an 'over-eager pest' rather than absent when deadlines approach so make-up and engraving resources can be mobilized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve archival material; don't clip bound volumes
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid snipping clippings from bound volumes, as this ruins the page and its reverse side for future reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the card index and bound volumes properly; spend extra time finding past issues instead of cutting clippings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruct accidents by combining sources and own observation
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine 'how it happened', take eyewitness statements (written), consult police and deputies, and use the reporter's own observation of vehicle damage to piece versions together, recognizing all conclusions are tentative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand limitations: most eyewitnesses see only the result; police versions are preliminary; 3,000 pounds of metal can move unpredictably; use coroner/medical examiner statements when death occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify vehicle ownership/operation and markings before assigning company responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume ownership or operation from markings (e.g., bus insignia); a vehicle carrying old markings may have been sold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check schedules, ownership, and registration before attributing a wreck to a particular company; accept nothing as final until verified by adding figures up, down, and crosswise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether to return to office or telephone in (cold accidents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Time factors determine whether the reporter returns to write the story or telephones information for a rewrite man; near deadlines telephone is likelier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Less experienced reporters should phone notes and let rewrite staff handle phrasing; an expert may dictate successfully but it's a different skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat police reports critically and attribute culpability to the source
rubrics_metrics.description: When covering an accident secondhand from police reports, apply the same verification care; police may guess names or allocate blame and the reporter should accredit such statements to the police.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer safer wording for potentially libelous statements: e.g., instead of 'The Johnson car failed to halt for an arterial stop-sign' write 'The police report said that the Johnson car apparently failed to halt for an arterial stop-sign.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Read police records alertly for hidden interest and avoid literalism
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer's sketchy description may mask an unusual accident; read reports alertly rather than randomly to spot potential distinctive stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow up on tantalizing details (e.g., child's doll carriage crushed) by interviewing officers, witnesses and involved parties to develop distinctive accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conservative casualty estimates for train wreck first-day stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone down casualty lists on the first day rather than exaggerate; using conservative estimates preserves credibility and gives subsequent stories new information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: announce 'Four killed' initially and later 'Six killed' rather than the reverse; some press associations cut estimates in half for first-day stories — a recommended practice for young reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain and verify the railroad casualty list
rubrics_metrics.description: Railroad officials can and should provide and revise casualty lists; the reporter should verify lists with hospitals and other sources because statuses can change rapidly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check hospital lists, conductors' lists and railroad revisions; railroad men will revise casualty lists readily in return for accurate information from reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train wreck reporting — what happened to passengers
rubrics_metrics.description: Gather information on what happened to the passengers of the wrecked train and how they were sent on to their destinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tangent often yields interesting two- or three-paragraph accounts (e.g., passengers forced to travel in inferior cars); follow-up reporting may expand into full features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train wreck reporting — traffic rerouting and adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: Report how traffic was rerouted or otherwise adjusted to prevent massing or blockades on either side of the wreck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe alternate routes, temporary measures and the strain on secondary lines, including operational difficulties (e.g., light rails flexing under heavy sleepers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Train wreck reporting — details of reopening the line
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the work of reopening the line to traffic (wrecking crews, cranes, delays) as it can be one of the most interesting parts of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain technical and logistical challenges (insufficient crane capacity, arrival times of heavier wreckers) and the actions of wrecking crews rather than inventing drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train wreck reporting — statements of survivors
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect speedy interviews with survivors for human-interest side-stories, ensuring they are genuine and informative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish valuable survivor recollections from trivial ones, and pursue human detail (e.g., honeymoon couple separated) to give the story humanness; verify identities for heroism stories, omit names for cowardice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train wreck reporting — prominent names and human drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Be alert for famous or prominent names and dramatic bits of heroism or cowardice which add human interest to wreck stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prominent individuals merit strong mention; seek names and verification for heroism accounts, but omit identifying details for alleged cowardice to avoid unfairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train wreck reporting — wreck sidelights and quirks
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for small, unusual sidelights (freak details) that give the story personality (e.g., mother clinging to a milk bottle despite losing shoes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These often come from interviewing and add vivid human detail; verify and include only accurate, attributable sidelights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train wreck reporting — statements by responsible railroad men
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect explanations or statements issued by responsible railroad officials, usually from general offices, to include the railroad perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such statements for second-day amplification but avoid using them as sole basis for cause until investigations proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train wreck reporting — report on freight cargo when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: If a wreck involved a freight train, report something of its cargo (perishables, cattle) and consequences (watering animals, spoilage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate shunting, sidetracking and alternate routing to explain secondary impacts beyond passenger casualties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drowning coverage — qualify warnings and avoid presumptive language
rubrics_metrics.description: When on-shore people claim they warned swimmers about rough water, qualify such claims unless convinced; avoid phrasing like 'was drowned' that implies external agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'said' to attribute warnings (e.g., 'Floyd Henneman and John Smiley said they had cautioned the boys that the lake was dangerously rough.') and avoid judgmental language about survivors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drowning coverage — refrain from judging survivors who saved themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not pass judgment on a survivor who saved himself while a companion drowned; rescuing another can be physically impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize difficult decisions and include full circumstances before assigning moral labels; gather rescue attempt details to comfort families and inform readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drowning coverage — gather full details of rescue attempts
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect details of who attempted rescues, how long artificial resuscitation was tried, and what was done clinically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These details are interesting to the public and comforting to families; avoid criticizing medical decisions about resuscitation without full facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire coverage — positioning and asking 'why'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not go inside burning buildings; position near commanding fire officers so you can learn the situation and the reasons for tactical actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask 'Why did the firemen break the windows on the north side but not the west?' — understanding tactics and building type (hardware store vs dry goods) is essential to write a helpful story for readers who will ask similar questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire coverage — verify casualty rumors immediately
rubrics_metrics.description: Rumors about loss of life or injuries spread quickly at fires; verify all such information before printing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm casualties with fire executives, hospitals or other authoritative sources rather than relying on crowd gossip.
